ahead.e: From a- + head. Perhaps originally a nautical term, beyond the head (of a ship), then drifting into more general English usage where it is used to describe something as being in front of.

s.d: having the leading position or higher score in a contest
x: he is ahead by a pawn
the leading team in the pennant race

s.d: at or in the front
x: I see the lights of a town ahead
the road ahead is foggy

s.d: toward the future; forward in time
x: I like to look ahead in imagination to what the future may bring
I look forward to seeing you

s.d: in a forward direction
x: go ahead
the train moved ahead slowly

s.d: ahead of time; in anticipation
x: when you pay ahead (or in advance) you receive a discount
We like to plan ahead

s.d: to a more advanced or advantageous position
x: a young man sure to get ahead
pushing talented students ahead

s.d: to a different or a more advanced time (meaning advanced either toward the present or toward the future)
x: moved the appointment ahead from Tuesday to Monday
pushed the deadline ahead from Tuesday to Wednesday

s.d: leading or ahead in a competition
x: the horse was three lengths ahead going into the home stretch
ahead by two pawns

s.d: At or towards the front; in the direction one is facing or moving.
x: The island was directly ahead.
Just ahead you can see the cliffs.

s.d: So as to be further advanced, either spatially or in an abstract sense; to be superior.
x: He finished two laps ahead of me.
In all of his classes Jack was ahead.

s.d: In or for the future.
x: There may be tough times ahead.
You've got to think ahead so as not to be unprepared.

s.d: To a later time.
x: Set the clock ahead an hour.
Push the deadline ahead a day, from the 20th to the 21st.

s.d: At an earlier time; beforehand; in advance.
x: He paid his rent ahead.

s.d: in an advantageous position
x: she's ahead of the game

s.d: before the usual time or the time expected
x: she graduated early
the house was completed ahead of time

s.d: the utterance of a sound similar to clearing the throat; intended to get attention, express hesitancy, fill a pause, hide embarrassment, warn a friend, etc.
To cough or clear one's throat so as to draw attention.
x: He wouldn't have been suspected of crying for the world, but he coughed and ahemmed, and finally turned away without speaking.

A full inspiration, preparatory to hawking, ahemming, or premeditated careful coughing, would excite an explosion of an unusually violent and persistent cough, hurrying the breath out of the poor victims.

s.d: The sound of a quiet cough or of clearing one's throat.
Demanding attention.
x: Ahem! Could we please get started?
Enter Nobody, and the Clowne. / Nobody. Ahem boy, Nobody is ſound yet for all his troubles.

s.d: Expresses disapproval or annoyance.
x: Ahem! In case you didn't notice, I did my share of the work, too.

s.d: Indicates the speaker does not wish to be perceived as rude, often intimating an impolite meaning to a third party that the speaker is not addressing.: Indicates subtle sarcasm, polite lying, or euphemism.
x: I really (ahem!) liked the chocolate broccoli surprise.

s.d: a Buddhist and Hindu and especially Jainist doctrine holding that all forms of life are sacred and urging the avoidance of violence
(uncountable) A doctrine of non-violence, concerned with the sacredness of all living things and an effort to avoid causing harm to them.
x: Already, at this very early date, the ritualists were moving towards the ideal of ahimsa ("harmlessness") that would become the indispensable virtue of the Indian Axial Age.
This, in essence, is the Jain doctrine of ahimsa – a direct inversion of Vedic beliefs about the sustaining powers of animal sacrifice.

s.d: unconcerned with or unrelated to history or to historical development or to tradition
Lacking historical perspective or context.
x: Students are profoundly ahistorical now, and I think they need to work out the notion of how their own environment, over time, has shaped their lives.

s.d: Not historically true or accurate; unsupported by historical evidence.
x: The American historian John van Engen argues that Le Goff's and Schmitt's idea of a semi-pagan medieval Europe filled with remnants of 'Indo-European folklore' is rather dogmatic and ahistorical.
